lines: A database vendor publishes a benchmark report showing their engine beating a competitor's by a wide margin.
Every single number in that report is independently reproducible, and every one of them is true.
A customer who goes on to adopt that engine purely on the strength of this report still finds it running slower than the competitor, on their own real workload.
So how exactly can every published number be true, and the overall comparison still manage to mislead someone reading it.
And what, sitting inside several vendors' own actual licence terms, would have stopped that competitor from publishing their own correction.
answer: Nothing in that report actually needs to be false.
Choosing carefully which true queries to publish, and which ones to quietly leave out, is benchmarketing, not fabrication.
And a licence term, named after one particular researcher, can genuinely forbid a competitor from publishing any benchmark result at all without the original vendor's own prior approval.

lines: Here is what two of the big industry suites each actually stress.
One has its own eight separate tables and twenty two queries, stressing broad, ad hoc analytical questions over a comparatively simple schema.
The other extends that same idea much further, to a far larger, deliberately skewed schema and ninety nine separate queries, closer to a real retail warehouse.
One single wide table. Forty three queries. No joins anywhere at all.
That makes it fast to run and remarkably easy to compare across many different engines.
The cost, stated plainly by the benchmark's own documentation, is that it tests absolutely nothing about join performance or multi table schema design.
This next benchmark is built on a real, correlated movie dataset, and quite deliberately so.
Cardinality estimates computed on simplifying assumptions like uniformity and independence turn out to be frequently wrong once you're looking at genuinely real data.
That is the exact same failure this very chapter already demonstrated once before, now scaled all the way up to a named, peer reviewed industry benchmark.
One particular industry specification was, by its own stated purpose, aimed squarely at data integration workloads rather than query execution.
That specification now sits listed, by the standards body's own current page, under its own table of obsolete workloads.

Benchmarketing means a vendor carefully choosing which true queries, which subset, or which particular configuration gets published, so that every number shown stays accurate while the overall comparison still quietly misleads.
A licence clause named for one specific researcher is a documented term that can forbid publishing any unsanctioned benchmark result at all.
An independently reproducible harness and baseline still matters even when a vendor's own number might genuinely be true, simply because it's the one thing neither of those two tricks can block.
Pulling this together now.
Each of those industry suites stresses something genuinely real, and quietly skips something else just as real.
Benchmarketing, and a licence clause that can silence a correction, are exactly the trap this entire chapter's own method exists to resist.
This chapter's own lab closes right here.
An honest load generator, a seeded data generator, and this very topic's own small, openly disclosed baseline, all published together and re-run end to end from one single command.
So what does a bundle like that actually prove.
answer: Not a sixth industry suite, comparable to the big five.
This bundle is small on purpose, and it says so plainly.
What it actually proves is the method itself: a properly warmed up target, honest load generation, genuinely representative data, and a result anyone else can re-run and check for themselves.
